title: Diving into dependen-“sea”
text:
How CRAN packages are interconnected
H. Sherry Zhang

2022-10-18
When writing a package, we may want to use functions in other packages. This creates a dependency for our package and a reverse dependency on the package we borrow functions from. As one of the recipients of the isoband email1, I’m curious to know how interconnected CRAN packages are. Luckily, it is not too hard to get data on this, and so the journey begins…

title: H. Sherry Zhang
text:
My research develops visualization methods and open-source software that make exploratory data analysis easier, more flexible, and more reliable. Modern statistical problems increasingly combine multiple data sources and data types, which places greater demands on data preparation, exploration, and visualization before confirmatory analysis. In applied work, I have found that the decisions behind a published analysis are often scattered across the manuscript, supplement, and code, making it difficult to piece them together or to explore how the results would change under alternative decisions. I therefore also study how large language models (LLMs) can help analysts document and extend these decisions, supporting both reproducibility and the exploration of alternatives.
Themes:

Tidy spatio-temporal data and glyph maps
Projection pursuit, the guided tour, and interactive graphics
Transparent data analysis with large language models






Many environmental and ecological data are collected repeatedly over time at fixed locations, and analyses need to move between the spatial and temporal components or study both at once. Much of the methodological work on such data focuses on modelling, but before and alongside modelling, analysts also need to explore the data: to see how temporal patterns vary across locations, to spot unusual locations or periods, and to check whether the data support a model’s assumptions. The glyph map is one visualization that shows both at once, drawing each location’s time series as a small plot at its geographic position. Figure 1 traces how my work brings glyph maps into the R ecosystem.








Figure 1: Poster presented at the ENVR Workshop 2026, Houston, Texas: Seeing space and time together: glyph maps in R. Download the PDF.





Selected work:

cubble: a tidy data structure for spatio-temporal data that lets analysts switch between spatial and temporal views, with a ggplot2 extension for glyph maps. Journal of Statistical Software, 2024; ASA John M. Chambers Statistical Software Award.  
sugarglider: extends glyph maps beyond line glyphs to ribbon and segment glyphs, developed by the undergraduate and master’s students I supervised in Google Summer of Code 2024. The R Journal, 2026.  
The ggplot2 extension ecosystem: an overview for users and developers, with Joyce Robbins (Columbia University) and Gina Reynolds (University of Denver). Invited submission to WIREs Computational Statistics, minor revision. 














High-dimensional data cannot be seen all at once, but they can be explored through a sequence of low-dimensional projections. A tour animates such a sequence, and projection pursuit guides it towards informative projections by optimizing an index function, which is often non-differentiable and can have local maxima. My work helps understand when this optimization succeeds or fails, by tracing optimizer paths in the projected and original spaces and by characterizing the index functions themselves.
Selected work:

Visual diagnostics for constrained optimisation with application to guided tours (ferrn). The R Journal, 2021.  
Squintability and other metrics for assessing projection pursuit indexes and guiding optimization choices, which also adds a swarm-based optimizer to the guided tour, with Jessica Leung and collaborators. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 2026. 
A tidy workflow for index composition (tidyindex): breaks index construction into building blocks, such as dimension reduction or distribution fitting, in the same way that tidymodels does for modeling, so that analysts can compare indexes, explore design choices, and quantify index uncertainty. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 2025.  
The state-of-the-art on tours for dynamic visualization of high-dimensional data, led by Stuart Lee. WIREs Computational Statistics, 2022. 
Maintainer, with Dianne Cook and Ian Lyttle, of the CRAN Task View: Dynamic Visualizations, a curated guide to R packages for dynamic and interactive graphics.





Building on a published analysis is often harder than it should be: the decisions behind a result are scattered across the manuscript, supplement, and code, and questions such as how the result would change under a different decision can be difficult to explore. With Roger Peng, I proposed a schema that records each decision and its rationale in plain language, from which LLMs can generate the analysis code. Because each decision is recorded as a separate step, alternative choices can be specified and turned into code, so that the alternatives can be compared directly (Figure 2). The schema keeps human judgment at the center of the analysis and leaves LLMs only the mechanical translation into code. We demonstrate it on a published regression analysis and on the many-analysts football study, where it also serves as a reproducibility check. Under review at the Annals of Applied Statistics. 








Figure 2: Overview of the schema-driven workflow. A schema is either authored manually or extracted from a manuscript by an LLM (left). To reproduce the analysis (top), an LLM generates code from the schema and validates it through iterative execution and repair in a sandboxed environment, and the analyst compares its estimates with those reported. To explore alternatives (bottom), an alternative file is merged with the schema to give one schema per alternative, each passed through the same generation and validation. Badges mark whether a step is performed by a human or an LLM.





Related work:

Inside Out: externalizing assumptions in data analysis as validation checks, with Roger Peng. Journal of Data Science, 2026. 
An LLM-based pipeline for understanding decision choices from published literature, applied to air pollution and mortality studies.

title: PhDone
text:
H. Sherry Zhang

2023-08-24



Today, I submitted my thesis! These three Wordle attempts summarise the three topics of my PhD research:

designing diagnostic plots for projection pursuit optimisation, applied to guided tour,
developing a spatio-temporal data structure in R and using glyph maps to visualise the data, and
proposing a data pipeline approach under the tidy framework to construct indexes.

Surprisingly (and hopefully), the last two words turned out to be actual Wordle solutions: “glyph” on 18th November 2022, and “index” on 15th August 2023 - just a few days before the submission deadline! Realising today’s Wordle solution is what I’ve been working on daily feels like stumbling upon the crossword clue “corolla leaf” 🌸, or in a more recent analogy, spotting the Adélie penguins in the Sea Life 🐧.
To see what I have been working on for the past 3.5 years, you can check out my thesis at https://sherryzhang-thesis.netlify.app/

title: How long do maps on ggplot facets take?
text:
If you’re a ggplot user, faceted plots must be under your belt. If you happen to do some spatial analysis, you can’t be more familiar with maps. Today, I will show you my findings on the rendering time of faceted map.
This example comes from Chapter 7 of Paula Moraga’s book Geospatial Health Data: Modeling and Visualization with R-INLA and Shiny and I have simplified it for my demonstration. In essence, there are two datasets:

The details on calculating SIR is not the focus of this post and Section 7.1 to 7.2 of Paula’s book has detailed all the steps you need if interested. Here I attach the script to generate these two data in case you would like to give it a spin:
What we would like to do here is to show those SIR values of each county on the map across year. This would require us to join the two datasets, supply the combined data into ggplot, plot the underlying map, fill the county polygon with SIR, make facets with year, and lastly add a few tweaks on theme and the scale of fill. Let’s give this plot a name, say target:
combined <- ohio %>% 
  left_join(sir, by = c("NAME" = "county"))

target <- combined %>% 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(aes(fill = SIR)) +
  facet_wrap(~year, dir = "h", ncol = 7) +
  ggtitle("SIR") + 
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    midpoint = 1, low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red"
  )

target
Easy peasy.
But, have you thought about how long it would take to bring this plot to you?

title: How long do maps on ggplot facets take?
text:
Footnotes


To make a proper benchmark of time, ideally each plot (p1 - p21) should be evaluated repetitively to obtain a distribution of the elapsed time. I set up a script with 50 repetitions and let it run overnight, but what I got next morning was “RStudio quit unexpectedly”. I suspect there is something going on with opening and closing the graphic devices too many times…↩︎

title: H. Sherry Zhang
text:
I am a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of Statistics and Data Science at the University of Texas at Austin, working with Roger Peng. My research develops visualization methods and software for exploring multivariate and spatio-temporal data, and uses large language models (LLMs) to document and extend the decisions behind a data analysis. My R package cubble won the 2024 ASA John M. Chambers Statistical Software Award. I received my PhD from Monash University in Australia in 2023 under the supervision of Dianne Cook, Patricia Menéndez, Ursula Laa, and Nicolas Langrené.

Read more about my research →
